First, it was noted that proposers in Kuali must not confuse a CASC “table” or "send back” with a rejection.

These steps are often taken when a relatively straightforward piece of additional supporting documentation is needed, and it does not generally presage rejection of a proposal.
Second, proposal quality matters and “overlap statements” must be thorough and substantiated.
Third, the CASC review is too late in the approval process for overlap concerns to be meaningfully addressed.
CASC has consistently and systematically tried to push this issue “down the chain” to the college and department curriculum committees where it can be better grappled with.
The overlap discussion highlighted for FSEC members the need for faculty to be trained in the curriculum process.

The online resources available tend to focus on the technical aspects of Kuali rather than on best practices in creating curricular proposals.

FSEC members offered wide-ranging comments on the report.
A stated goal in the report was to significantly increase graduate enrollment but faculty are right to be skeptical about how this might come to pass.
Many departments have experienced declines in their full-time faculty lines and wonder where the resources will come from to support this increase.
Other suggestions, like eliminating the Graduate Council’s role in the course approval process seem to run counter to the long-standing principle of faculty involvement in curricular matters.
Assertions about “branding” also seem misguided as graduate programs tend to attract their students via college- or department- specific outreach and not through an overarching administrative unit.
A number of other practical considerations would seem to limit the report’s stated aspirations.
These include recent decreases and eliminations in federal funds (and unpredictable access to existing funds), and limits on international students’ ability to access programs.

There is also a lot of uncertainty around the university’s roll out of a new budget model and its proposal to create a medical school.
These works in progress make it difficult to gauge the potential success of the report’s recommendations.

Guests: Christopher Lavan, Assoc.
Vice Provost for Advancement of Teaching and Learning, and Assoc.
Professor of Education Shane Tutwiler, Chair, Joint Committee for Academic Program Review and Outcomes Assessment (JAPROA) joined the meeting.
AVP Lavan started off by outlining the work of the ATL office, noting that it supports the work of committees like JAPROA and JCODL in an advisory and consultative way.
Some history and background was provided on the work of prior iterations of these committees and by former key staffers in the ATL office.
AVP Lavan and Chair Tutwiler stressed that the faculty-led committees retain the authority to conduct reviews within well-established processes, but the scope of that authority seems to confuse some faculty members.
It was noted that JAPROA is a newer committee that only experienced its first full operational year in AY24-25.

Committee members too struggled with the line between “advising” and “approving.” In short, when an undergraduate program is proposed by a department or college, the outcomes assessment portion of that proposal is assigned to JAPROA, which undertakes its work with assistance from the ATL office.
Also, the office has been developing a “Manual” or handbook that outlines the academic program review process which should become a valuable resource for departments undergoing reviews.
Chair Tutwiler noted that the guidance is drawn from Chapter 8 of the University Manual and the committee is keenly interested in simplifying the process to make it easier for departments to undertake.
He considers the work of his committee to be invaluable in guiding metaprocesses and ensuring that the university, through all aggregated academic units, continues to learn from self-study and reflection, and therefore improves and succeeds.
While JAPROA’s role involves providing feedback on outcomes assessments, they can only adopt and forward recommendations, but the final decisions always rest in the departments.

Wrapping up, FSEC members suggested that the draft manual be shared with the membership, and the committees might consider a graphic presentation of their workflows and processes which might enhance understanding. 4.

Priority Items 3.1 Suggestions for FS nominations to a search committee for the new Athletic Director- Two nominees have been submitted. 3.2 Future of the Budget and Administration Committee - It was noted that the committee had been created in response to the university’s transition to a new budget model and the need for information about that process to flow to faculty.
Now that the university has sunset its administrative committee responsible for providing guidance and advice during the transition, it is unclear what how the BAC should focus its efforts.
It has no administrative counterpart and no clear nexus of cooperation with key administrators.

Past President Walls noted that models from peer institutions were used in developing the legislation that created the BAC.
Faculty-forward institutions like Tufts have a long history of having a permanent, standing committee responsible for weighing in on budget matters.
Given that implementation details of the new budget model remain unavailable, it was agreed that new processes and procedures still hold the potential to negatively impact faculty (through program consolidations and other potential outcomes).
It thus seems important to keep the committee active.
It was noted that a retired faculty member for many years tracked revenues by source, especially state support for the university, and university expenditures.
Continuation of such tracking might be a worthwhile task for a committee of faculty.
The Committee also serves to act as a second set of eyes on decision making and is a formal body that can hear faculty concerns and advocate on their behalf.
Uncertainty around the person or office that should serve as a contact or administration representative for the Committee has been a source of frustration.
